claim: The samples were taken at Helgoland Island about 40 km offshore in the southeastern North Sea in the German Bight at the station 'Kabeltonne' (54° 11.3' N, 7° 54.0' E).
source: The samples were taken at Helgoland Island about 40 km offshore in the southeastern North Sea in the German Bight at the station 'Kabeltonne' (54° 11.3' N, 7° 54.0' E; Figure 1) between the main island and the minor island, Düne (German for 'dune').
evidence: Direct statement of sampling location with specific coordinates

claim: Water depths at the sampling site fluctuate from 6 to 10 m over the tidal cycle.
source: Water depths at this site fluctuate from 6 to 10 m over the tidal cycle.
evidence: Direct measurement of water depth at the sampling location

claim: During most of the year, a westerly current transports water from the English Channel alongside the Dutch and Frisian coast to Helgoland.
source: During most of the year, a westerly current transports water from the English Channel alongside the Dutch and Frisian coast to Helgoland, but water around the island is also influenced by nutrient inputs from the rivers Weser and Elbe and from the northern North Sea (Wiltshire et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited reference to previous work describing water circulation patterns

claim: During the 2009 to 2012 study period, the lowest water temperatures were measured in mid to late February with a minimum of 1.1°C in 2010 and maximum of 3.4°C in 2009.
source: During the 2009 to 2012 study period, the lowest water temperatures were measured in mid to late February (min. 2010: 1.1°C; max. 2009: 3.4°C), followed by a continuous increase until a peak in August (min. 2011: 18.0°C; max. 2009: 18.7°C) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct temperature measurements reported in supplementary data

claim: Water temperatures peaked in August with a minimum of 18.0°C in 2011 and maximum of 18.7°C in 2009.
source: During the 2009 to 2012 study period, the lowest water temperatures were measured in mid to late February (min. 2010: 1.1°C; max. 2009: 3.4°C), followed by a continuous increase until a peak in August (min. 2011: 18.0°C; max. 2009: 18.7°C) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct temperature measurements reported in supplementary data

claim: Spring phytoplankton blooms in the North Sea typically develop during March and reach highest intensities during April and May.
source: Spring phytoplankton blooms in the North Sea typically develop during March and reach highest intensities during April and May.
evidence: Observational data from the study period

claim: The highest chlorophyll a concentrations during spring blooms are usually observed at the coastlines including the area around Helgoland Island.
source: The highest chlorophyll a concentrations are usually observed at the coastlines including the area around Helgoland Island (Figure 2).
evidence: Satellite imagery showing chlorophyll a distribution referenced in Figure 2

claim: At Helgoland island, spring phytoplankton blooms started around mid March when water temperatures surpassed 3 to 5°C.
source: At Helgoland island, spring phytoplankton blooms started around mid March when water temperatures surpassed 3 to 5°C (Figure 3A–H; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Temperature and bloom timing data shown in figures and supplementary files

claim: The diatoms Chaetoceros debilis, Chaetoceros minimus, Mediopyxis helysia, Rhizosolenia styliformis, Thalassiosira nordenskioeldii, the silicoflagellate Chattonella, the haptophyte Phaeocystis and dinoflagellates dominated spring blooms in terms of cell numbers.
source: The diatoms Chaetoceros debilis and Chaetoceros minimus, Mediopyxis helysia, Rhizosolenia styliformis and Thalassiosira nordenskioeldii, the silicoflagellate Chattonella, the haptophyte Phaeocystis and dinoflagellates dominated these blooms in terms of cell numbers (Figure 3I–L; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Microscopic cell count data presented in figures and supplementary files

claim: Phaeocystis spp. cells have estimated biovolumes of approximately 50 to 250 µm³.
source: Spherical Phaeocystis spp. cells for example have estimated biovolumes of ~50 to 250 µm3, whereas elipsoid cylindrical Mediopyxis helysia cells have a biovolume of ~82,000 µm3 and for Rhizosolenia styliformis even a biovolume of ~282,000 µm3 has been reported (Olenina, 2006; Loebl et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited biovolume measurements from previous studies

claim: Mediopyxis helysia cells have a biovolume of approximately 82,000 µm³.
source: Spherical Phaeocystis spp. cells for example have estimated biovolumes of ~50 to 250 µm3, whereas elipsoid cylindrical Mediopyxis helysia cells have a biovolume of ~82,000 µm3 and for Rhizosolenia styliformis even a biovolume of ~282,000 µm3 has been reported (Olenina, 2006; Loebl et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited biovolume measurements from previous studies

claim: Rhizosolenia styliformis has a biovolume of approximately 282,000 µm³.
source: Spherical Phaeocystis spp. cells for example have estimated biovolumes of ~50 to 250 µm3, whereas elipsoid cylindrical Mediopyxis helysia cells have a biovolume of ~82,000 µm3 and for Rhizosolenia styliformis even a biovolume of ~282,000 µm3 has been reported (Olenina, 2006; Loebl et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited biovolume measurements from previous studies

claim: All blooms were accompanied by a notable decrease of silicate.
source: All blooms were accompanied by a notable decrease of silicate (Figure 3A–D; Supplementary file 1), which diatoms use for frustule formation (see Yool and Tyrrell (2003) for the controlling effect of silicate on diatom abundance).
evidence: Silicate measurements shown in figures and supplementary data

claim: Diatoms use silicate for frustule formation.
source: All blooms were accompanied by a notable decrease of silicate (Figure 3A–D; Supplementary file 1), which diatoms use for frustule formation (see Yool and Tyrrell (2003) for the controlling effect of silicate on diatom abundance).
evidence: Established biological knowledge cited from previous work

claim: Bloom maximum intensities decreased from 2009 to 2012 with chlorophyll a maxima reaching 28 mg m⁻³ (day 82) in 2009, 18 mg m⁻³ (day 125) in 2010, 15 mg m⁻³ (day 116) in 2011, and 11 mg m⁻³ (day 114) in 2012.
source: Bloom maximum intensities decreased from 2009 to 2012 with chlorophyll a maxima (measured by fluorescence) reaching 28 mg m-3 (day 82), 18 mg m-3 (day 125), 15 mg m-3 (day 116), and 11 mg m-3 (day 114) in each respective year (Figure 3A–D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Chlorophyll a measurements from fluorescence data

claim: In 2009, bacterioplankton peaked at 3.5×10⁶ cells ml⁻¹ on day 118, 36 days after the chlorophyll a maximum.
source: In 2009, the bacterioplankton peaked at 3.5x106 cells ml-1 (day 118), 36 days after the Chl a maximum.
evidence: Cell count data from microscopy

claim: In 2010, the bacterioplankton peak abundance was 2.4×10⁶ cells ml⁻¹ on day 129, four days after the chlorophyll a peak.
source: In 2010, the peak in Chl a was broader and only four days ahead of the bacterioplankton peak abundance of 2.4x106 cells ml-1 (day 129).
evidence: Cell count data from microscopy

claim: In 2011, the bacterioplankton peak abundance was 2.3×10⁶ cells ml⁻¹ on day 118, two days after the chlorophyll a peak.
source: In 2011, the Chl a peak was only two days ahead of the bacterioplankton peak abundance of 2.3x106 cells ml-1 (day 118), whereas it was nine days ahead in 2012, where the bacterioplankton peaked at 3.2x106 cells ml-1 (day 123).
evidence: Cell count data from microscopy

claim: In 2012, the bacterioplankton peaked at 3.2×10⁶ cells ml⁻¹ on day 123, nine days after the chlorophyll a peak.
source: In 2011, the Chl a peak was only two days ahead of the bacterioplankton peak abundance of 2.3x106 cells ml-1 (day 118), whereas it was nine days ahead in 2012, where the bacterioplankton peaked at 3.2x106 cells ml-1 (day 123).
evidence: Cell count data from microscopy

claim: SAR11 dominated the bacterioplankton community in winter.
source: DAPI and CARD-FISH cell staining (Supplementary files 3 and 4) showed that SAR11 dominated the bacterioplankton community in winter, but with the onset of each spring bloom relative abundances of Bacteroidetes followed by Gammaproteobacteria increased and finally surpassed those of the SAR11 (Figure 3M–P).
evidence: CARD-FISH cell count data

claim: With the onset of each spring bloom, relative abundances of Bacteroidetes followed by Gammaproteobacteria increased and finally surpassed those of SAR11.
source: DAPI and CARD-FISH cell staining (Supplementary files 3 and 4) showed that SAR11 dominated the bacterioplankton community in winter, but with the onset of each spring bloom relative abundances of Bacteroidetes followed by Gammaproteobacteria increased and finally surpassed those of the SAR11 (Figure 3M–P).
evidence: CARD-FISH cell count data showing temporal dynamics

claim: Bacteroidetes reached higher maximum relative abundances than Gammaproteobacteria, 40% (2012) to 60% (2010) as compared to 10% (2012) to 30% (2010), respectively.
source: Bacteroidetes reached higher maximum relative abundances than Gammaproteobacteria, 40% (2012) to 60% (2010) as compared to 10% (2012) to 30% (2010), respectively.
evidence: CARD-FISH relative abundance data

claim: Bacteroidetes genera Polaribacter, Formosa, and VIS6 peaked each year with relative abundances well above 5%, reaching relative abundances of up to 25% sometimes within less than a week.
source: Bacteroidetes genera Polaribacter, Formosa, and VIS6, a genus-level clade within the family Cryomorphaceae (Gómez-Pereira et al., 2010), peaked each year with relative abundances well above 5%, reaching relative abundances of up to 25% sometimes within less than a week (Figure 3Q–T).
evidence: CARD-FISH abundance data showing rapid increases

claim: VIS6 is a genus-level clade within the family Cryomorphaceae.
source: Bacteroidetes genera Polaribacter, Formosa, and VIS6, a genus-level clade within the family Cryomorphaceae (Gómez-Pereira et al., 2010), peaked each year with relative abundances well above 5%, reaching relative abundances of up to 25% sometimes within less than a week (Figure 3Q–T).
evidence: Taxonomic classification cited from previous work

claim: Ulvibacter reached similar peak abundances to Polaribacter, Formosa, and VIS6 with the exception of 2012, where this genus never surpassed 2% and ranged below 1% most of the time.
source: Ulvibacter reached similar peak abundances with the exception of 2012, where this genus never surpassed 2% and ranged below 1% most of the time.
evidence: CARD-FISH abundance data showing inter-annual variation

claim: Within Gammaproteobacteria, the genus-level SAR92 clade responded notably in all years increasing from background levels below 1% to relative abundance of 8% to 16%.
source: Within Gammaproteobacteria the genus-level SAR92 clade responded notably in all years increasing from background levels below 1% to relative abundance of 8% to 16%.
evidence: CARD-FISH abundance data showing consistent response across years

claim: Members of the Alteromonadales families Alteromonadaceae and Colwelliaceae bloomed in three years (2010: 8%; 2011: 6%; 2012: 7%).
source: Members of the Alteromonadales families Alteromonadaceae and Colwelliaceae bloomed in three (2010: 8%; 2011: 6%; 2012: 7%), and genus Reinekea in two (2009: 16%; 2010: 5%) of the years (Figure 3U–X).
evidence: CARD-FISH abundance data

claim: Genus Reinekea bloomed in two years (2009: 16%; 2010: 5%).
source: Members of the Alteromonadales families Alteromonadaceae and Colwelliaceae bloomed in three (2010: 8%; 2011: 6%; 2012: 7%), and genus Reinekea in two (2009: 16%; 2010: 5%) of the years (Figure 3U–X).
evidence: CARD-FISH abundance data

claim: The genus Balneatrix within Gammaproteobacteria reached relative abundances up to 2%.
source: Some less abundant, but nevertheless recurrent taxa included the genus Balneatrix within Gammaproteobacteria with relative abundances up to 2% (Figure 3U–X).
evidence: CARD-FISH abundance data

claim: The NS3a marine group reached 9% abundance in 2009 and 6% in 2011.
source: Minor recurring groups of Bacteroidetes (Figure 3Y-β) included the NS3a marine group (9% in 2009 and 6% in 2011), the genus-level VIS1 clade within the NS5 marine group detected before the Chl a peaks of 2011 (7%) and 2012 (5%), and the Cytophagia clade Marinoscillum that reached 1–3% abundance most years after initial blooms.
evidence: CARD-FISH abundance data

claim: The genus-level VIS1 clade within the NS5 marine group was detected before the chlorophyll a peaks of 2011 (7%) and 2012 (5%).
source: Minor recurring groups of Bacteroidetes (Figure 3Y-β) included the NS3a marine group (9% in 2009 and 6% in 2011), the genus-level VIS1 clade within the NS5 marine group detected before the Chl a peaks of 2011 (7%) and 2012 (5%), and the Cytophagia clade Marinoscillum that reached 1–3% abundance most years after initial blooms.
evidence: CARD-FISH abundance data with temporal context

claim: The Cytophagia clade Marinoscillum reached 1–3% abundance most years after initial blooms.
source: Minor recurring groups of Bacteroidetes (Figure 3Y-β) included the NS3a marine group (9% in 2009 and 6% in 2011), the genus-level VIS1 clade within the NS5 marine group detected before the Chl a peaks of 2011 (7%) and 2012 (5%), and the Cytophagia clade Marinoscillum that reached 1–3% abundance most years after initial blooms.
evidence: CARD-FISH abundance data

claim: Relative proportions of 16S tags from distinct clades correlated for the most part with those inferred from CARD-FISH cell counts.
source: Relative proportions of 16S tags from distinct clades correlated for the most part those inferred from CARD-FISH cell counts (Figure 4A–P), but members of SAR11 were substantially underreported - a known limitation of the 806R primer used in V4 amplification for 2010 to 2012 samples (Apprill et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison of two independent methods with cited primer bias

claim: Members of SAR11 were substantially underreported in 16S tag sequencing, which is a known limitation of the 806R primer used in V4 amplification.
source: Relative proportions of 16S tags from distinct clades correlated for the most part those inferred from CARD-FISH cell counts (Figure 4A–P), but members of SAR11 were substantially underreported - a known limitation of the 806R primer used in V4 amplification for 2010 to 2012 samples (Apprill et al., 2015).
evidence: Known technical limitation cited from previous work

claim: The Flavobacteriia genus Tenacibaculum bloomed in 2010 with read frequencies of max. ~12% and in 2011 with max. ~5%.
source: Additional abundant clades detected in the 16S amplicon data comprised the Flavobacteriia genus Tenacibaculum (Figure 4U–X) that bloomed in 2010 (read frequencies of max. ~12%) and 2011 (max. ~5%).
evidence: 16S rRNA gene tag sequencing data

claim: 'Candidatus Planktomarina temperata' (DC5-80-3 lineage) reached 6–21% of the tag data.
source: Within the alphaproteobacterial Rhodobacteriaceae, high abundances of 'Candidatus Planktomarina temperata' (DC5-80-3 lineage) and the NAC11-7 clade were detected reaching 6–21% and 7–19% of the tag data, respectively (Figure 4U–X).
evidence: 16S rRNA gene tag sequencing data

claim: The NAC11-7 clade reached 7–19% of the tag data.
source: Within the alphaproteobacterial Rhodobacteriaceae, high abundances of 'Candidatus Planktomarina temperata' (DC5-80-3 lineage) and the NAC11-7 clade were detected reaching 6–21% and 7–19% of the tag data, respectively (Figure 4U–X).
evidence: 16S rRNA gene tag sequencing data

claim: Within Alphaproteobacteria, the genus Sulfitobacter peaked with a read frequency of ~7% in 2010.
source: Also within Alphaproteobacteria the genus Sulfitobacter peaked with a read frequency of ~7% in 2010 (Figure 4V), and within Betaproteobacteria the order Methylophilales (dominated by OM43 clade members) was detected with high relative abundances of up to ~10% before blooms, which decreased with bloom progression.
evidence: 16S rRNA gene tag sequencing data

claim: Within Betaproteobacteria, the order Methylophilales (dominated by OM43 clade members) was detected with high relative abundances of up to ~10% before blooms, which decreased with bloom progression.
source: Also within Alphaproteobacteria the genus Sulfitobacter peaked with a read frequency of ~7% in 2010 (Figure 4V), and within Betaproteobacteria the order Methylophilales (dominated by OM43 clade members) was detected with high relative abundances of up to ~10% before blooms, which decreased with bloom progression.
evidence: 16S rRNA gene tag sequencing data showing temporal dynamics

claim: Verrucomicrobia were detected with decreasing peak read frequencies of 7.7% (2010), 5.0% (2011) and 2.9% (2012).
source: Verrucomicrobia (Figure 4U–X) were detected with decreasing peak read frequencies of 7.7% (2010), 5.0% (2011) and 2.9% (2012).
evidence: 16S rRNA gene tag sequencing data showing temporal trend

claim: The decrease in Verrucomicrobia corresponds to decreasing bloom intensities, which supports a proposed role of Verrucomicrobia in polysaccharide decomposition.
source: This decrease corresponds to decreasing bloom intensities, which supports a proposed role of Verrucomicrobia in polysaccharide decomposition (e.g. Martinez-Garcia et al., 2012).
evidence: Correlation between observed data and cited hypothesis

claim: Eleven clades peaked during at least two of the four spring blooms with relative cell abundances or read frequencies ≥5%.
source: Within Bacteroidetes, Gammaproteobacteria and Rhodobacterales a total of eleven clades peaked during at least two of the four spring blooms with relative cell abundances or, for those clades that were not assessed by CARD-FISH, relative read frequencies ≥5%.
evidence: Summary of CARD-FISH and 16S tag sequencing data

claim: The eleven recurrent clades were six Flavobacteriia clades (Formosa, Polaribacter, NS3a marine group, Tenacibaculum, Ulvibacter, VIS6 clade Cryomorphaceae), three Gammaproteobacteria clades (Alteromonadaceae/Colwelliaceae, Reinekea and SAR92), and two Roseobacter clades (DC5-80-3 and NAC11-7).
source: These were six Flavobacteriia clades (Formosa, Polaribacter, NS3a marine group, Tenacibaculum, Ulvibacter, VIS6 clade Cryomorphaceae), three Gammaproteobacteria clades (Alteromonadaceae/Colwelliaceae, Reinekea and SAR92), and two Roseobacter clades (DC5-80-3 and NAC11-7).
evidence: Summary of abundance data across multiple years

claim: Each year a succession was observed within the Flavobacteriia and Gammaproteobacteria clades.
source: Each year a succession was observed within the Flavobacteriia and Gammaproteobacteria clades.
evidence: Temporal patterns observed in abundance data

claim: The succession in the Flavobacteriia was more pronounced than in the Gammaproteobacteria, but the sequence of clades varied.
source: The succession in the Flavobacteriia was more pronounced than in the Gammaproteobacteria, but the sequence of clades varied.
evidence: Comparison of temporal patterns between bacterial classes

claim: The abundances of the most prominent Flavobacteriia clades were for the most part correlated with multiple algae groups and physiochemical factors.
source: Spearman rank correlation analyses revealed that the abundances of the most prominent Flavobacteriia clades were for the most part correlated with multiple algae groups and physiochemical factors (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis results

claim: According to linear regression analyses, the strongest abiotic predictors were temperature, salinity, silicate and nitrate.
source: According to linear regression analyses, the strongest abiotic predictors were temperature, salinity, silicate and nitrate, and the strongest biotic predictors were Phaeocystis spp. haptophytes, Rhizosolenia spp., Chaetoceros debilis, and Chaetoceros minimus diatoms and the silicoflagellate Chattonella (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Statistical regression analysis results

claim: According to linear regression analyses, the strongest biotic predictors were Phaeocystis spp. haptophytes, Rhizosolenia spp., Chaetoceros debilis, and Chaetoceros minimus diatoms and the silicoflagellate Chattonella.
source: According to linear regression analyses, the strongest abiotic predictors were temperature, salinity, silicate and nitrate, and the strongest biotic predictors were Phaeocystis spp. haptophytes, Rhizosolenia spp., Chaetoceros debilis, and Chaetoceros minimus diatoms and the silicoflagellate Chattonella (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Statistical regression analysis results

claim: In no case was a simple one-to-one relationship between specific algae and specific bacterioplankton groups detected.
source: It should be noted though that linear regressions were computed based on log-transformed abundance data and not algae volumes (which were not measured). Thus, the influence of the rather small cell-sized algae such as Chaetoceros minimus is likely overestimated. Such limitations notwithstanding it is noteworthy that in no case a simple one-to-one relationship between specific algae and specific bacterioplankton groups was detected.
evidence: Statistical analysis results with methodological caveats

claim: The Ulvibacter clade was positively correlated with diatoms and haptophytes and negatively correlated with silicoflagellates.
source: The strongest significant (p<0.05) correlations were obtained for the Ulvibacter clade that was positively correlated with diatoms and haptophytes and negatively correlated with silicoflagellates.
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis with significance testing

claim: Polaribacter abundance was correlated with Chattonella abundances.
source: Further results comprised an opposite trend for the VIS1 clade of the NS5 marine group, and a correlation of Polaribacter and Chattonella abundances (see Supplementary file 6 for details).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis

claim: In total, 16 metagenomes of free-living bacterioplankton (0.2–3 µm) were generated from time points before, during and after spring phytoplankton blooms.
source: In total, 16 metagenomes of free-living bacterioplankton (0.2–3 µm) were generated from time points before, during and after spring phytoplankton blooms, six during 2009 using the 454 FLX Ti platform that were published previously (Teeling et al., 2012) and ten during 2010–2012 using the Illumina HiSeq2000 platform.
evidence: Description of sequencing dataset

claim: Six metagenomes were generated during 2009 using the 454 FLX Ti platform.
source: In total, 16 metagenomes of free-living bacterioplankton (0.2–3 µm) were generated from time points before, during and after spring phytoplankton blooms, six during 2009 using the 454 FLX Ti platform that were published previously (Teeling et al., 2012) and ten during 2010–2012 using the Illumina HiSeq2000 platform.
evidence: Description of sequencing methods with citation

claim: Ten metagenomes were generated during 2010–2012 using the Illumina HiSeq2000 platform.
source: In total, 16 metagenomes of free-living bacterioplankton (0.2–3 µm) were generated from time points before, during and after spring phytoplankton blooms, six during 2009 using the 454 FLX Ti platform that were published previously (Teeling et al., 2012) and ten during 2010–2012 using the Illumina HiSeq2000 platform.
evidence: Description of sequencing methods

claim: The 454 and Illumina metagenomes were deeply sequenced with final assembled contigs of up to 96 kbp and 458 kbp, respectively.
source: Most of the 454 (0.5–4 pico titer plates / metagenome) and all of the Illumina metagenomes (1 lane / metagenome; 2x150 bp) were deeply sequenced (Supplementary file 8) with final assembled contigs of up to 96 kbp and 458 kbp, respectively.
evidence: Sequencing depth and assembly statistics

claim: Taxonomic classification of the metagenome contigs resulted in identification of major bloom-associated clade sequence bins including Formosa, Polaribacter, the NS3a and NS5 marine groups, and Cryomorphaceae of the Flavobacteriia and Alteromonadales, Reinekea, Glaciecola and the SAR92 clade of the Gammaproteobacteria.
source: Taxonomic classification of the metagenome contigs resulted in identification of major bloom-associated clade sequence bins (Supplementary file 9), including Formosa, Polaribacter, the NS3a and NS5 marine groups, and Cryomorphaceae of the Flavobacteriia and Alteromonadales, Reinekea, Glaciecola and the SAR92 clade of the Gammaproteobacteria.
evidence: Bioinformatic taxonomic classification of metagenomic sequences

claim: Classification was poor for Ulvibacter (Flavobacteriia) and Balneatrix (Gammaproteobacteria), most likely since the only available reference genomes were too distant from North Sea representatives.
source: Classification was poor, however, for Ulvibacter (Flavobacteriia) and Balneatrix (Gammaproteobacteria), most likely since the only available reference genomes (unidentified eubacterium SCB49; Balneatrix alpica) were too distant from North Sea representatives.
evidence: Bioinformatic classification results with inferred explanation

claim: Clone libraries from 2009 indicated 16S rRNA similarities of only 94% for Ulvibacter and 91% for Balneatrix to available reference genomes.
source: Clone libraries from 2009 (Teeling et al., 2012) indicated 16S rRNA similarities of only 94% and 91%, respectively, for these two clades.
evidence: 16S rRNA gene similarity data from previous study

claim: Reinekea was mostly represented by distinct clusters in GC content versus coverage plots.
source: We plotted contig GC contents versus coverage to evaluate our taxonomic classification, which in some cases allowed to assess the coherence of some of the clades (Figure 5). For example, Reinekea (Figure 5D,H,I) and the NS5 marine group (Figure 5H,L,M,O) were mostly represented by distinct clusters, whereas Polaribacter (Figure 5D,H,I) was almost always represented by at least two clusters indicating the presence of sub-populations.
evidence: Metagenomic assembly analysis visualized in GC-coverage plots

claim: The NS5 marine group was mostly represented by distinct clusters in GC content versus coverage plots.
source: We plotted contig GC contents versus coverage to evaluate our taxonomic classification, which in some cases allowed to assess the coherence of some of the clades (Figure 5). For example, Reinekea (Figure 5D,H,I) and the NS5 marine group (Figure 5H,L,M,O) were mostly represented by distinct clusters, whereas Polaribacter (Figure 5D,H,I) was almost always represented by at least two clusters indicating the presence of sub-populations.
evidence: Metagenomic assembly analysis visualized in GC-coverage plots

claim: Polaribacter was almost always represented by at least two clusters in GC content versus coverage plots, indicating the presence of sub-populations.
source: We plotted contig GC contents versus coverage to evaluate our taxonomic classification, which in some cases allowed to assess the coherence of some of the clades (Figure 5). For example, Reinekea (Figure 5D,H,I) and the NS5 marine group (Figure 5H,L,M,O) were mostly represented by distinct clusters, whereas Polaribacter (Figure 5D,H,I) was almost always represented by at least two clusters indicating the presence of sub-populations.
evidence: Metagenomic assembly analysis with interpretation of population structure

claim: The number of clusters increased from pre-bloom to mid-bloom situations and decreased slightly towards late bloom situations and notably towards post-bloom situations.
source: In general, the number of clusters increased from pre-bloom to mid-bloom situations and decreased slightly towards late bloom situations and notably towards post-bloom situations.
evidence: Temporal pattern observed in GC-coverage cluster analysis

claim: This tendency of increasing then decreasing cluster numbers was more evident in 2009, the year with the highest bloom intensity and the largest number of metagenome samples spanning a broader timespan.
source: This tendency was more evident in 2009, the year with the highest bloom intensity and the largest number of metagenome samples spanning a broader timespan (Figure 5A–F).
evidence: Comparison of temporal patterns across years with different sampling densities

claim: High in situ abundance did not always correlate with good metagenome assemblies.
source: It is noteworthy that high in situ abundance did not always correlate with good metagenome assemblies.
evidence: Observation from comparing abundance and assembly quality data

claim: SAR11, while highly abundant in all metagenome datasets, yielded few large contigs, possibly due to population heterogeneity and presence of hyper-variable regions described in sequenced SAR11 genomes.
source: SAR11 for example, while highly abundant in all metagenome datasets, yielded few large contigs, possibly due to population heterogeneity and presence of hyper-variable regions described in sequenced SAR11 genomes (Wilhelm et al., 2007).
evidence: Assembly results with inferred explanation based on cited genomic features

claim: Increases in Flavobacteriia relative abundance during blooms was always accompanied by an increase in community-wide CAZyme gene frequency as well as an increase in the diversity of CAZyme families.
source: Analyses of functional genes identified in the bacterioplankton metagenomes revealed that increases in Flavobacteriia relative abundance during blooms was always accompanied by an increase in community-wide CAZyme gene frequency as well as an increase in the diversity of CAZyme families (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Metagenomic functional gene analysis showing correlation

claim: As blooms subsided, CAZyme frequencies also declined.
source: As blooms subsided, CAZyme frequencies also declined. This was most pronounced for more densely sampled years in 2009 and 2010.
evidence: Temporal pattern in metagenomic functional gene frequencies

claim: The 20 glycoside hydrolase families with the highest mean abundances during bloom dates were, in descending order, GH3, 23, 13, 16, 103, 73, 92, 2, 17, 30, 5, 20, 36, 65, 29, 1, 42, 31, 81, and 18.
source: The 20 glycoside hydrolase families with the highest mean abundances during bloom dates were, in descending order, GH3, 23, 13, 16, 103, 73, 92, 2, 17, 30, 5, 20, 36, 65, 29, 1, 42, 31, 81, and 18 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Metagenomic CAZyme family abundance analysis

claim: The abundant GH families are indicative for the hydrolysis of certain glucans, xylans, mannans (GH92), cellulose (GH5), fucans (GH29), and peptidoglycan (GH23, 103, 73, and 18).
source: While most of these families comprise a diverse range of functions, they are indicative for the hydrolysis of certain glucans, xylans, mannans (GH92), cellulose (GH5), fucans (GH29), and peptidoglycan (GH23, 103, 73, and 18).
evidence: Functional annotation based on CAZy database knowledge

claim: The abundant families GH3, 16, 17 and 5 comprise β-1,3-glucanases and the family GH30 β-1,6-glucanases, which are involved in the cleavage of chrysolaminarin.
source: The abundant families GH3, 16, 17 and 5 comprise β-1,3-glucanases and the family GH30 β-1,6-glucanases. Both enzymes are involved in the cleavage of chrysolaminarin.
evidence: Functional annotation based on CAZy database knowledge

claim: Chrysolaminarin is a mostly linear β-1,3-glucan with occasional β-1,6 branches and is the storage polysaccharide in diatoms.
source: Chrysolaminarin, a mostly linear β-1,3-glucan with occasional β-1,6 branches, is the storage polysaccharide in diatoms and thus one of the most abundant polysaccharides on Earth.
evidence: Established biochemical knowledge about diatom polysaccharides

claim: Chrysolaminarin is one of the most abundant polysaccharides on Earth.
source: Chrysolaminarin, a mostly linear β-1,3-glucan with occasional β-1,6 branches, is the storage polysaccharide in diatoms and thus one of the most abundant polysaccharides on Earth.
